new.title: Tour Edmond Rostand's neo-Basque Villa Arnaga
new.desc: Villa Arnaga is the neo-Basque house that Cyrano de Bergerac author Edmond Rostand designed himself and moved into in 1906. It stands in 15 hectares of French and English-style gardens and has been owned by the town since 1962. It carries the Maisons des Illustres label.
new.tip: Opening hours vary by season, so check arnaga.com first. Allow time for the gardens as well as the house.
new.q: Villa Arnaga, Route du Docteur Camino, Cambo-les-Bains

new.title: Visit the cliff-top Château d'Abbadia in Hendaye
new.desc: Neo-Gothic castle-observatory built from 1864 for the explorer and astronomer Antoine d'Abbadie, with Viollet-le-Duc credited as architect. It stands on the cliffs above the Basque coast and was left to the Académie des Sciences, which still owns it. The observatory worked until 1975.
new.tip: Visits are guided and booking is advised; the grounds and coastal paths around it are the best part on a clear day.

new.title: Walk around the Vauban fort at Socoa
new.desc: Fort de Socoa guards the entrance to the bay of Saint-Jean-de-Luz. Work began under Henri IV, the Spanish held it in 1636, and Vauban later remodelled it. It is a listed monument and now belongs to the local communauté de communes.
new.tip: Access to the interior is limited, but the base of the fort has a good panorama of the bay. Combine it with the quay and beach of Socoa.

new.title: See the baroque altarpiece of Saint-Jean-Baptiste
new.desc: This church in Saint-Jean-de-Luz is where Louis XIV married the Infanta Maria Theresa of Austria on 9 June 1660. Its gilded baroque retable fills the choir, and the nave has the typical Basque wooden galleries. It is listed as a monument historique.
new.tip: Enter from rue Gambetta and look up at the galleries. Guided tours by the Pays d'art et d'histoire run on set dates.

new.title: Step inside the house where Louis XIV stayed in 1660
new.desc: Lohobiague-Enea, known as Maison Louis XIV, was built in 1643 for the shipowner Joannis de Lohobiague. Louis XIV lodged here in 1660 before his wedding. Visits are guided, with a maximum of about 20 to 25 people at a time.
new.tip: Seasonal opening; check maison-louis-xiv.fr. The house is on place Louis XIV, beside the harbour.
new.q: Maison Louis XIV, Place Louis XIV, Saint-Jean-de-Luz

new.title: Look at the Maison de l'Infante on the quay
new.desc: This brick-and-stone house on the harbour in Saint-Jean-de-Luz sheltered the Spanish Infanta Maria Theresa before her marriage to Louis XIV in 1660. It faces the Maison Louis XIV across the port quarter.
new.tip: The house is best admired from the quay; check with the tourist office for visit days.
new.q: Maison de l'Infante, Quai de l'Infante, Saint-Jean-de-Luz

new.title: Stroll the main street of Ainhoa
new.desc: Ainhoa is a bastide-type village on the border of Labourd and Navarre, founded in the Middle Ages to host pilgrims heading to Santiago de Compostela. It is a member of Les Plus Beaux Villages de France, with white houses and red or green timbering lining one street.
new.tip: Park at the entrance and walk the single street. Pair it with Espelette and Sare, which are close by.

new.title: Photograph the pepper-draped houses of Espelette
new.desc: Espelette is the home of the AOP piment d'Espelette. Its Labourd houses have white walls and red or green timber framing, and strings of peppers hang from the façades to dry from late summer into autumn. The village has a 17th and 18th century core.
new.tip: Come between September and October for the full display of drying peppers. Weekday mornings are quieter.

new.title: Wander through the Basque village of Sare
new.desc: Sare is a Labourd village at the foot of La Rhune, near the Spanish border, and is listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France. It is the base for the Rhune rack railway and the prehistoric caves.
new.tip: Sit on the fronton square, then continue to the caves or the train at Col de Saint-Ignace.

new.title: Descend into the Grottes de Sare
new.desc: Limestone cave system at Sare with a developed route, an audio-visual guided tour of around 45 minutes to an hour, a museum and a megalithic park. The tour covers geology, prehistoric habitation and Basque origins, and runs in French, English, Basque and Spanish.
new.tip: Book date, time and language online. It is open all year apart from a short winter closure, so confirm before going.

new.title: Climb to the Vauban citadel of Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port
new.desc: The 17th-century citadel stands on the site of the old Navarrese royal castle, on the highest point of the town. Vauban inspected the town in 1680 and 1685. It now houses a school, but the cobbled climb up rue de la Citadelle gives a wide view over the town and hills.
new.tip: Guided citadel visits run on selected dates. Walk up from the old town through the Porte Saint-Jacques.

new.title: Tour the Château de Pau, birthplace of Henri IV
new.desc: The Château de Pau is a national museum and domain, with a tapestry collection that includes eight pieces sent by Louis-Philippe in 1842. It became a national museum in 1929 and holds about 12,000 works and objects.
new.tip: Check the museum website for closing days. Pair it with a walk along the Boulevard des Pyrénées.
new.q: Château de Pau, Rue du Château, Pau

new.title: Watch the Pyrenees from the Boulevard des Pyrénées
new.desc: Pau's panoramic promenade, opened between the château and the Palais Beaumont between 1893 and 1899, has a view of the Pyrenees from the Pic du Midi de Bigorre to the Pic du Midi d'Ossau on clear days. A viewing table helps name the peaks.
new.tip: Go at sunset on a clear day. The funicular from the station arrives right here.

new.title: Study the Romanesque portal of Oloron cathedral
new.desc: The Cathédrale Sainte-Marie in Oloron-Sainte-Marie keeps a sculpted Romanesque portal from about 1120 to 1140, sheltered by a bell-tower porch. Its tympanum shows the rare theme of the Descent from the Cross. It is part of the UNESCO Camino de Santiago routes in France.
new.tip: Look closely at the tympanum figures. The building is now a parish church and is free to enter.
new.q: Cathédrale Sainte-Marie, Place de la Cathédrale, Oloron-Sainte-Marie

new.title: Walk the 16th-century ramparts of Navarrenx
new.desc: Navarrenx got its bastide charter in 1316, and its bastioned walls were started in 1538 under Henri d'Albret by the Italian engineer Fabricio Siciliano. The walls are about 1.66 km long and are classified monuments. The town held out in a siege in 1569.
new.tip: The ramparts are free to walk; a loop of about 45 minutes is signposted. Visits led by the tourist office run in summer.

new.title: Cross the medieval Pont Vieux at Orthez
new.desc: The Pont Vieux dates from the 13th and 14th centuries, begun under Gaston VII de Moncade when he made Orthez the capital of Béarn. It has a tower, uneven arches and has been a listed monument since 1875. The Tour Moncade, remnant of the castle, stands nearby.
new.tip: Walk it from the old town side, then continue to the Tour Moncade.

new.title: Visit the salt spring crypt in Salies-de-Béarn
new.desc: Salies-de-Béarn's brine is about ten times saltier than seawater. The Place du Bayaà has covered the town's salt spring since 1865, and a crypt beneath it, built to protect the source, can be visited. A salt museum in a 17th-century house tells the story.
new.tip: Combine the crypt with the Musée du Sel; check the Béarn des Gaves tourist office for hours.

new.title: Climb the Tour Monréal at Sauveterre-de-Béarn
new.desc: The Tour Monréal is a tower over 30 metres tall on a rocky outcrop above the Gave d'Oloron. Sources date it to the 12th or 13th century, and it has been a museum since 2016. A riverside path leads down to the Pont de la Légende.
new.tip: Walk down the stairs to the Pont de la Légende and the Île de la Glère afterwards.

new.title: Ride the train to the Marquèze ecomuseum
new.desc: Marquèze is an open-air museum in the Landes de Gascogne regional park, created in 1969, recreating 19th-century life in the Grande Lande. It is reached only by a small train from the former Sabres station and covers nearly 20 hectares. It is a Musée de France.
new.tip: Seasonal: one guide lists 1 April to 27 September. Check marqueze.fr and allow half a day.

new.title: See sculpture in the Donjon Lacataye, Mont-de-Marsan
new.desc: The Donjon Lacataye is a keep of the old castle, dated to the 14th or 15th century, and a listed monument since 1942. Since 1968 it has housed the Musée Despiau-Wlérick, devoted to sculptors Charles Despiau and Robert Wlérick of Mont-de-Marsan.
new.tip: Opening hours were affected by works, so check beforehand. The address is Place Marguerite de Navarre.
new.q: Donjon Lacataye, Place Marguerite de Navarre, Mont-de-Marsan

new.title: Watch steam rise at Dax's Fontaine Chaude
new.desc: The Fontaine Chaude is a monument over the source of the Nèhe spring, built 1814 to 1818 and listed since 1946. The water comes out at about 60 degrees and is still used by the town's thermal baths. Legend says a Roman legionnaire's dog was cured here.
new.tip: It is free and open in the city centre. Come on a cold morning to see the steam.
new.q: Fontaine Chaude, Place de la Fontaine Chaude, Dax

new.title: Find the Pas de Roland rock arch at Itxassou
new.desc: The Pas de Roland is a natural rock passage cut by the Nive near Itxassou, tied to the legend of the knight Roland. It is free and open at all times and is reached on foot, about 2 km from the village, as part of loops such as the walk to Atharri.
new.tip: Park in the village, as the road has no space. Wear shoes that cope with mud.

new.title: Look up at the limestone peaks of Cirque de Lescun
new.desc: The Cirque de Lescun is a glacial amphitheatre in the Vallée d'Aspe, inside the Pyrénées National Park. The village of Lescun sits at about 900 m on its slope, and the GR10 passes through. The Pic d'Anie and Pic du Billare rise above it.
new.tip: Drive up from Oloron in about 45 minutes. Most trails start from the Anapia car park.

new.title: Find Maurice Ravel's birthplace on Ciboure's quay
new.desc: The house at 27 quai Maurice Ravel in Ciboure is where the composer was born on 7 March 1875. A shipowner built it in 1630, and Cardinal Mazarin stayed there in 1660 before Louis XIV's wedding. It is a listed monument and visible from outside only.
new.tip: The interior is not open; look at it from the quay. Ciboure's old streets behind it are worth a wander.
new.q: Maison de Ravel, 27 quai Maurice Ravel, Ciboure

new.title: Tour the 14th-century Château d'Urtubie
new.desc: Château d'Urtubie in Urrugne, about 3 km from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, dates from 1341 and has stayed in the same family. It is a listed monument with tapestries and a park, and also runs as a hotel.
new.tip: Visits are paid and seasonal; check chateaudurtubie.net. The nearby coast is a short drive.

new.title: Taste a mouchou at Maison Pariès
new.desc: Pariès is a Basque confectioner on rue Gambetta in Saint-Jean-de-Luz, known for the mouchou, a soft almond cake (muxu means kiss in Basque), plus touron and kanougas. The house dates from 1895.
new.tip: Buy mouchous and take a sit-down tea in the salon. Expect queues in summer.

new.title: Buy Basque macarons at Maison Adam
new.desc: Maison Adam claims its macarons were served at Louis XIV's wedding in 1660 and that the recipe has passed down orally since then, through about 13 generations. The shop sits on place Louis XIV in Saint-Jean-de-Luz.
new.tip: Try the classic Basque macaron, which is soft and chewy rather than crisp. Eat it fresh, as it softens in a day.
new.q: Maison Adam, Place Louis XIV, Saint-Jean-de-Luz

new.title: Graze the covered market of Saint-Jean-de-Luz
new.desc: Les Halles on boulevard Victor Hugo sell line-caught fish, sheep cheese, gâteau basque and piment d'Espelette. A buvette inside serves oysters with wine. The covered market is open every morning, with extra outdoor stalls on Tuesdays and Fridays.
new.tip: Arrive before 1 pm when stalls thin out. Buy a sheep cheese and a gâteau basque for a picnic.
new.q: Les Halles, Boulevard Victor Hugo, Saint-Jean-de-Luz

new.title: Book a modern Basque tasting menu at Le Kaïku
new.desc: Le Kaïku is a one-star Michelin restaurant at 17 rue de la République, a short walk from the port. Chef Nicolas Borombo trained at the Crillon and the George V and cooks modern Basque dishes with local produce. Gault&Millau gives it 15/20.
new.tip: Reservation is needed, and it is closed Sunday and Monday according to listings. Expect roughly 58 to 128 euros per person.
new.q: Le Kaïku, 17 rue de la République, Saint-Jean-de-Luz

new.title: Dine at the starred Ithurria inn in Ainhoa
new.desc: Ithurria is a family-run one-star Michelin inn on the Place du Fronton in Ainhoa, with chef Martin Isabal in the kitchen (Gault&Millau). Menus in the 2026 season run from 85 to 125 euros.
new.tip: Book ahead. Combine it with a walk along Ainhoa's main street.

new.title: Eat farm-to-table at Lore Ttipia, Auberge Ostapé
new.desc: Lore Ttipia is the one-star restaurant of Auberge Ostapé, a 17th-century farmstead on a country estate above Bidarray. Michelin describes modern cooking with farm-to-table produce, and Monday to Wednesday there is a simpler bistronomic menu.
new.tip: Michelin shows it as a high price bracket. Book ahead; the bistronomic Monday-Wednesday menu is the cheaper way in.
new.q: Auberge Ostapé, Domaine de Chahatoenia, Bidarray

new.title: Taste Ossau-Iraty sheep cheese at Ferme Agerria
new.desc: Ferme Agerria in Saint-Martin-d'Arberoue is a family farm where the visit ends with a tasting of AOP Ossau-Iraty sheep's-milk cheese. It is one of many farms on the Ossau-Iraty cheese route.
new.tip: Reservation is advised; the visit was priced around 6.50 euros for adults.

new.title: Taste Basque chocolate at Puyodebat in Cambo
new.desc: Chocolaterie Puyodebat in Cambo-les-Bains, on avenue de Navarre, combines a chocolate workshop, a museum and a shop. Founded by Christophe Puyodebat, it is recommended by tourism guides as Cambo's chocolate address.
new.tip: Try the traditional Basque chocolates. Cambo also celebrates gâteau basque each autumn.
new.q: Chocolaterie Puyodebat, Avenue de Navarre, Cambo-les-Bains

new.title: Taste Irouléguy wine at the Cave d'Irouléguy
new.desc: The cooperative cellar at Saint-Étienne-de-Baïgorry offers guided visits of the cellar and barrel room, ending with a tasting of the full range of Irouléguy cuvées. Slots run at 10:30 and 14:30, take about 1h30, and cost about 15 euros.
new.tip: Booking is mandatory. Phone +33 5 59 37 41 33 or check cave-irouleguy.com for dates.

new.title: Sip Williams pear eau-de-vie at Maison Brana
new.desc: Brana has made wine and spirits in Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port since 1897. Its tasting offer covers the distillery in Ossès, a shop on Place Floquet in the old town and the estate at Ispoure. The Williams pear eau-de-vie is the flagship.
new.tip: Check brana.fr for visits and hours. The shop in the old town is the easiest stop.

new.title: Taste dry and sweet Jurançon at Domaine Cauhapé
new.desc: Domaine Cauhapé at Monein works about 50 ha of steep vineyards and makes dry and sweet Jurançon. Winalist lists a 30-minute tasting of five cuvées and a one-hour visit with tasting, both free for groups of up to 20.
new.tip: Visits are by appointment, so phone +33 5 59 21 33 02 beforehand.

new.title: Try the Coucougnettes du Vert Galant at Francis Miot
new.desc: Francis Miot is a Pau confectioner, born in 1948, whose Coucougnettes are almonds in dark chocolate, rolled in marzipan flavoured with raspberry, ginger and Armagnac. They nod to Henri IV, nicknamed the Vert Galant. The Pau boutique is on rue Maréchal Joffre.
new.tip: Buy a box in the Pau shop, or visit the workshops in Uzos.
new.q: Maison Francis Miot, 46 rue Maréchal Joffre, Pau

new.title: Shop for Béarn produce at Les Halles de Pau
new.desc: Pau's covered market has been on the same site since 1927, was renovated in 2018 and has about 40 local vendors focused on Béarn products. It has two floors with food and eating options.
new.tip: Open Tuesday to Saturday 7 am to 1 pm and Sunday 9 am to 1 pm; the Nocturne evening opening is on the last Friday of the month.
new.q: Les Halles de Pau, Place de la République, Pau

new.title: Taste Bas-Armagnac at Domaine d'Ognoas
new.desc: The departmental Domaine d'Ognoas covers about 650 ha in Bas-Armagnac and has the oldest still in Gascony, from 1804, in a listed old cellar. The guided visit with tasting costs about 5 euros, and the shop sells Armagnac and Floc de Gascogne.
new.tip: Hours change with the season, with only Tuesdays listed for October to December 2026. Check tourismelandes.com before driving.

new.title: Order the day's catch at Goustut in Capbreton
new.desc: Goustut is a fish-focused restaurant on the port of Capbreton run by chef Charles Guillou. Gault&Millau puts the price at 34 to 70 euros per person without drinks. The port still lands the fish it serves.
new.tip: Book for dinner in season; look at the daily fish choices.

new.title: Buy fish and eat it at Chez Vincent Côté Océan
new.desc: Chez Vincent Côté Océan in Capbreton is both a fishmonger and a restaurant near the harbour. It is listed by Tourisme Landes among the port's restaurants serving locally landed fish.
new.tip: Check opening days with the restaurant; the port also has a daily fish market nearby.
new.q: Chez Vincent Côté Océan, 4 rue du Port d'Albret, Capbreton

new.title: Buy fish straight off the boats in Capbreton
new.desc: Capbreton fishermen sell their catch on the quay every day, from 9 am to noon and 3 pm to 6 pm, without a fish auction. The custom goes back to a decree of Colbert that exempted Capbreton fishermen from the criée.
new.tip: Go in the morning to see the choice. Ask what was landed that day.
new.q: Marché aux poissons, Quai de la Pêcherie, Capbreton

new.title: Eat duck at the Ferme Auberge Le Vieux Chêne
new.desc: Le Vieux Chêne is a farm inn in Castelnau-Chalosse that serves duck foie gras, magret, confit, garbure and salade landaise, with pasta made from farm wheat. It seats about 60 and is closed from December to February.
new.tip: Outside winter it serves lunch at weekends; booking is advisable.
new.q: Ferme auberge Le Vieux Chêne, 960 route de Dax, Castelnau-Chalosse

new.title: Ride the cog railway up La Rhune
new.desc: The Petit train de la Rhune is a rack railway that has run from the Col de Saint-Ignace in Sare to the 905 m summit since 1924. The climb takes about 35 minutes, and it is one of four rack railways in service in France. New track was laid in 2023.
new.tip: A return fare was listed at about 26 euros for adults. Take a jacket, as the summit is windier than the coast.
new.q: Train de la Rhune, Col de Saint-Ignace, Sare

new.title: Watch surfers at La Gravière in Hossegor
new.desc: La Gravière is one of the best-known beach breaks in Hossegor, heavy close to shore and tidal, and listed among the town's four world-class surf spots. The best surfers compete in Hossegor's autumn world championship stop.
new.tip: Go in autumn or winter for the biggest waves. Park near the central beach and walk five minutes.

new.title: Learn to surf at Les Estagnots in Seignosse
new.desc: Les Estagnots is the best-known beach at Seignosse for surf, a supervised Blue Flag beach that hosts a world championship stage. Surf schools such as Surf Seignosse Paradise and Esta Surf School operate here. Summer swell is gentle enough for beginners.
new.tip: Book a school lesson in summer; experienced surfers come in autumn.

new.title: Swim at Navarrosse on Lac de Biscarrosse
new.desc: Navarrosse is a supervised sandy beach lined by pines on the freshwater lake shared by Biscarrosse, Parentis, Gastes and Sainte-Eulalie. The lake is fed by the Canal des Landes and is not tidal, so swimming is possible at any hour.
new.tip: Parking is paid in summer and only the left part of the beach is supervised.

new.title: Glide down the Courant d'Huchet in a galupe
new.desc: Boatmen at Léon take visitors in flat-bottomed galupes along the seven-kilometre Courant d'Huchet, which winds through dunes, bogs, pines and cork oaks to the sea at Moliets. Private boats, paddles and canoes are banned, so a guided boat is the only way.
new.tip: Runs April to October. Bateliers: +33 5 58 48 75 39, site bateliers-courant-huchet.fr.
new.q: Bateliers du Courant d'Huchet, Lac de Léon, Léon

new.title: Cycle the Vélodyssée from Parentis to Mimizan-Plage
new.desc: The Vélodyssée stage from Parentis-en-Born to Mimizan-Plage is about 31 km and takes around two hours by bike. It crosses the Sainte-Eulalie state forest and stops at the small port of Piaou before reaching the ocean.
new.tip: The route passes a campsite closed at night, with listed gate hours. Rent bikes at Cycles en Born in Mimizan-Plage.

new.title: Hike from Gourette via the Bézou gondola
new.desc: Gourette is a Pyrenean ski resort in the Ossau valley that is also used for summer hiking. The Bézou gondola runs from late June to 31 August and lets walkers start at altitude; the easy Bergerie walk takes about an hour.
new.tip: Check the gondola's summer schedule before setting off. The GR10 gives a walk back down to the resort.

new.title: Ride the Petit train d'Artouste to 2,000 m
new.desc: The Petit train d'Artouste is reached by gondola from the Lac de Fabrèges and runs a loop of about 10 km in 55 minutes at 2,000 m. It was created in 1924 for dam works and has carried tourists since the 1930s. From the arrival, the lake is a 20 to 30 minute walk.
new.tip: Runs May to October. Download your tickets in advance, as mobile coverage at Fabrèges is weak, and bring warm clothing.
new.q: Télécabine d'Artouste, Lac de Fabrèges, Laruns

new.title: Take the free funicular up to the Boulevard des Pyrénées
new.desc: The Pau funicular links the railway station to the Boulevard des Pyrénées in the upper town. It dates from 1908 and is free to use, running every few minutes.
new.tip: Check that it is running, as one article reported it out of service.
new.q: Funiculaire de Pau, Place de la Gare, Pau

new.title: Join the Fête du Piment in Espelette
new.desc: The Fête du Piment d'Espelette is held on the last weekend of October, with the 2026 edition on 24 and 25 October. Access is free and the village fills with stalls, processions and tastings.
new.tip: Arrive early, as the village draws crowds. Check the programme with the town hall or the Confrérie.

new.title: Swim on the Grande Plage in Hendaye
new.desc: Hendaye's Grande Plage is a supervised beach with views across the Bidassoa to Jaizkibel in Spain. Surf schools operate here, and the beach suits both beginners and experienced surfers.
new.tip: Lifeguards patrol from June to September. Cycle tracks link the beach to the port and the Deux Jumeaux.

new.title: Swim on the sheltered Grande Plage of Saint-Jean-de-Luz
new.desc: The Grande Plage is protected by a crescent of three sea walls, Artha, Sainte-Barbe and Socoa, built in the late 19th century. The beach is about a kilometre long, between the port and the Pergola quarter. In summer a boat shuttles from the Digue aux Chevaux to Socoa.
new.tip: The sheltered water is good for families. Walk the promenade to Sainte-Barbe at sunset.

new.title: Watch the surf at Parlementia in Guéthary
new.desc: Guéthary is a village on the cliffs known for its reef waves. Parlementia, shared with Bidart, is a famous surf wave and a sandy beach supervised in summer, while Cenitz is the gentler neighbour.
new.tip: Watch from the cliff or village. Lifeguards are present in July and August.

new.title: Start the coastal path at Erretegia beach, Bidart
new.desc: Erretegia is a wilder, gravel-sand beach near Bidart centre, in a green setting, and the start of the coastal path to Hendaye, about 25 km. It has surf schools, lifeguards in summer and a small snack bar.
new.tip: Reach it by bus or a short path with steps. The sentier du littoral beyond has closed sections, so check before long walks.

new.title: Watch espadrilles made at Armaité
new.desc: Armaité is an espadrille workshop at Idaux-Mendy, near Mauléon-Licharre, the espadrille capital of the Basque Country. The visit lasts 30 to 45 minutes and costs about 4 euros per person, by appointment.
new.tip: Book on 05 59 28 33 61. Don Quichosse in Mauléon also has a workshop shop.

new.title: Take the waters at the Thermes de Cambo-les-Bains
new.desc: The thermal baths of Cambo-les-Bains use sulphur- and zinc-rich water that emerges at 22 degrees, recommended for rheumatology and respiratory care. The baths also welcome visitors who are not on a cure, with baths and water jets.
new.tip: Check the Chaîne Thermale du Soleil website for prices and season dates.

new.title: Walk to the Holzarté suspension footbridge
new.desc: The Passerelle d'Holzarté is a 70 m suspension footbridge above the Olhadubi gorge near Larrau, built in 1920 for woodcutters. It stands about 140 to 180 m above the gorge, depending on the source, and the wooden deck was replaced with metal.
new.tip: The classic walk is about 1.9 km and an hour, with 183 m of ascent. Start from the Larrau car park.

new.title: Join the Fêtes de la Madeleine in Mont-de-Marsan
new.desc: The Fêtes de la Madeleine are Mont-de-Marsan's July feria, five days and nights of concerts, parades and bullfights around the Arènes du Plumaçon and the town centre. The 2026 edition ran 22 to 26 July.
new.tip: Dates change each year; check tourismelandes.com or the Régie des fêtes for the programme and tickets.

new.title: Walk from the Deux Jumeaux to Pointe Sainte-Anne
new.desc: An easy walk starts at the Deux Jumeaux station in Hendaye and heads to the Pointe Sainte-Anne, with viewpoints over the Deux Jumeaux rocks. The rocks lie off the Abbadia estate and can be reached at low tide.
new.tip: Go at low tide. The old Corniche path across Ciboure, Urrugne and Hendaye was closed by a 2021 order, so keep to the signed route.
